passages.title: Quraysh's security and the call to worship
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These four ayat take one visible, everyday fact of Makkan life — the Quraysh's two great trading caravans and the safety they enjoyed on the road — and turn it into an argument for worshipping Allah alone. The unit is a single sentence in shape: a favour named (ayat 1–2), a command that follows from it (ayah 3), and the favour spelled out in its two essentials, food and safety (ayah 4). Nothing here is abstract. Allah points at their bread and their security and says: the One who gave you these is the One who deserves your worship.

## The bridge from Sūrah al-Fīl

Ibn Kathir notes that this sūrah was separated from the one before it in the primary Mushaf — the original copy of ʿUthmān — and the Companions wrote "In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" on the line between the two. Yet, he says, this sūrah is directly related to the one preceding it, as Muhammad bin Ishaq and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam both clarified. The joint meaning of the two runs: "We have prevented the Elephant from entering Makkah and We have destroyed its people in order to gather (*Ilāf*) the Quraysh, which means to unite them and bring them together safely in their city."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same closeness: all commentators concur that the subject-matter of the two sūrahs is so bound together that in some copies of the Qurʼān they had been written as a single sūrah without a *bismillāh* between them — until Sayyidunā ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him) compiled the standard copy with the consensus of the Companions, separated the two sūrahs and inserted the *bismillāh* between them.

So read ayah 1 with Sūrah al-Fīl still sounding in the ear. On this reading, the destruction of that army was not a stray event; it served the gathering of a people and their safety in their own city.

## Ayah 1: the one particle the scholars weighed

The sūrah opens with a preposition — *li-īlāfi Quraysh*, "for the *Ilāf* of Quraysh." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that by the rules of Arabic grammar this particle *li* has to be linked to some other sentence. Which one? The exegetes give different possibilities, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out three.

**First**, keeping in view the close relation of this sūrah with the previous one, some supply the unstated sentence "We destroyed the people of the elephant" — so that the Quraysh, familiar with their two commercial trips of winter and summer, would face no obstacle in them, and through that trading activity might develop a certain prestige, so that people would respect them.

**Second**, a second school takes the unstated word to be "Be amazed!" — one should wonder at the Quraysh undertaking winter and summer journeys freely and safely. Ibn Kathir reports Ibn Jarīr taking this same line: "The correct opinion is that the letter *Lām* is a prefix that shows amazement. It is as though He (Allah) is saying, 'You should be amazed at the uniting (or taming) of the Quraysh and My favour upon them in that.'" Ibn Jarīr adds that this follows from the consensus of the Muslims that these are two separate and independent sūrahs.

**Third**, a third school reads it as the *lām of taʿlīl* — the "because" *lām* — attached not backwards but forwards, to ayah 3: *because of* this familiarity and security, "they must worship the Lord of this House."

These readings do not fight each other so much as layer. Whether the favour is traced back to the elephant, held up for wonder, or made the direct reason for worship, the destination is the same command in ayah 3.

## The word *Ilāf*

Everything in ayat 1–2 turns on this one word, and it is worth slowing down for. The tafsirs give it a spread of senses that overlap:

- **Uniting and gathering.** Ibn Kathir: to *gather* the Quraysh means "to unite them and bring them together safely in their city." A scattered people made one.
- **Taming.** Ibn Jarīr's phrasing — "the uniting (or taming) of the Quraysh" — carries the sense of something made settled.
- **Familiarity, habit.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the opening "Because of the familiarity of the Quraish": the settled custom of two annual journeys, year after year.
- **What they gathered.** Ibn Kathir also reports that *Ilāf* refers to what they would accumulate on their journeys — winter to Yemen, summer to Ash-Shām — through trade and other than that.

Put together, the word names a mercy most people never notice: the mercy of the ordinary running smoothly. Allah draws their attention to the thing so reliable they had stopped seeing it.

## Ayah 2: two journeys, and why two

*"Their Ilāf caravans, in winter and in summer."* Ibn Kathir gives the two directions: winter to Yemen, summer to Ash-Shām. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the plain reason — Syria was a cold region, so they went there in summer; Yemen had a warm climate, so they went there in winter.

Why did they have to travel at all? Because Makkah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, is situated in an utterly bleak and arid valley where no agricultural produce grows, nor are there orchards from which its people could reap fruit. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets this beside the prayer of the founder of the House of Allah, Sayyidunā Ibrāhīm Khalīlullāh (peace be upon him), at the time of founding the city: *"My Lord, make this a city of peace, and provide its people with fruits"* (2:126) — and beside the ayah *"to which the fruits of everything are drawn"* (28:57). The Quraysh, it concludes, thus needed to make these commercial trips out of Makkah into the neighbouring territories to bring the necessities of life to their city.

**Hāshim's initiative.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from Sayyidunā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that the people of Makkah were in a state of abject poverty, and that Hāshim — the great-grandfather of the Prophet ﷺ — exhorted the Quraysh to undertake trading caravans to the neighbouring territories. Hāshim was the leader of Quraysh, and he maintained the economic principle of distributing the gains and profits of their business among the rich and the poor members of Quraysh alike, so that even the poor lived like the wealthy.

**Why they were never robbed.** Both tafsirs give the same reason, and it is the heart of the passage. They would return to their city safely because of the respect people had for them — Ibn Kathir: because they were the residents of Allah's sanctuary; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: because they were its keepers and custodians. Whoever knew them would honour them. And — a striking detail both give — even those who came to them and travelled with them would be safe because of them. Their protection spilled over onto their companions on the road.

This safety was not only for the road. For their life in the city, Ibn Kathir cites: *"Have they not seen that We have made it a secure sanctuary, while men are being snatched away from all around them?"* (29:67). Outside, people were being seized; inside, they were secure.

**A further favour.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Allah later spared them even the trouble of these annual trips: the areas adjacent to Makkah — Yemen, Tabālah and Harsh — were made fertile and productive, growing grain and other produce abundantly, even beyond their need, which was then carried to Jeddah and sold there. So most necessities were available in Jeddah, and the Makkans could go two stations there instead of undertaking two long journeys. The favour did not stay static; it grew easier.

## Ayah 3: the conclusion — *so let them worship*

*"So, let them worship the Lord of this House."* Ibn Kathir: after this magnificent favour, Allah directs them to be grateful — meaning "then let them single Him out for worship, just as He has given them a safe sanctuary and a Sacred House." He pairs it with the Prophet's ﷺ own commanded position: *"I have been commanded only to worship the Lord of this city, Who has sanctified it and to Whom belongs everything. And I am commanded to be from among the Muslims"* (27:91).

**Why "the Lord of this House" and not another name?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers precisely: having mentioned the divine favours, the Quraysh are especially enjoined to express their gratitude to "the Lord of this House" — and out of many attributes of Allah this one is singled out "because it was this House that became the source and fountain of all blessings for them." Their prestige, their safe passage, their trade, their food — all of it flowed from being the people of that House. So Allah addresses them by the very title that made their case unanswerable.

Notice, too, where the command lands. Allah does not say "worship this House"; He says worship **the Lord of** this House. Ibn Kathir draws the line explicitly: they should single Him out for worship alone, without any partner, and "should not worship any idol, rival or statue besides Him." The sanctuary is honoured; the honour belongs to its Owner.

## Ayah 4: hunger and fear

*"Who has fed them against hunger, and has made them safe from fear."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this ayah "comprehensively captures all that was needed for the Quraish to live happily and peacefully in the world." Two clauses cover a whole life:

- **Fed against hunger** — implying that they were provided all year round with every kind of fruit and food.
- **Made safe from fear** — including security from enemies and robbers, who out of their respect for them as guardians of the Kaʿbah spared them from their attacks; and, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, security from the punishment of the Hereafter, for those who fulfilled the necessary conditions of faith.

Ibn Kathir's comment on the same phrase: "He favours them with safety and gentleness, so they should single Him out for worship alone, without any partner." And he draws out the consequence in both directions: whoever accepts this command, Allah will give him safety in both this life and the Hereafter; whoever disobeys Him, He will remove both of them from him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same point from Ibn Kathir under its "Special Note".

**The illustration that follows.** Both sources then cite, as Allah's own illustration of this principle, the ayat of Sūrah an-Naḥl: a township that dwelt secure and well-content, its provision coming to it in abundance from every place, which then denied the favours of Allah, so Allah "made it taste extreme of hunger and fear, because of that which they used to do" — and there had come to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him, so the torment overtook them while they were wrongdoers (16:112–113).

The pairing is pointed. The two gifts named in ayah 4 are exactly the two the township lost — food and safety — and it lost them by ingratitude for them.

## The standing of Quraysh

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from the sūrah that Quraysh, of all the tribes of Arabia, was most acceptable in the sight of Allah, and cites two narrations.

The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: **"Verily, Allah selected Kinānah from the offspring of Prophet Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him) and selected Quraish from the progeny of Kinānah. From the Quraish, Allah selected Banū Hāshim and from Banū Hāshim He selected me."** — Baghawī, on the authority of Wāthilah Ibn Asqaʿ.

And another Tradition reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"People will follow Quraish in matters of good as well as in matters of evil."** — Muslim, on the authority of Jābir, as quoted by Mazharī.

Mazharī's own comment is worth keeping: the reason for the selection of the tribes named in the first narration is presumably on account of their special abilities, innate capacities and natural endowments. Even in the days of paganism and ignorance, when people practised kufr and shirk, their morals and inborn abilities were of a very high standard, and they had the perfect capacity to accept the truth — which is why most of the blessed Companions and Friends of Allah were Qurayshites.

## A note on reciting this sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records under "A Great Benefit" that Abul Hasan Qazwīnī stated that anyone who fears his enemy or an affliction should recite Sūrah al-Quraysh, and it will give him security from fear and calamity. Imām Jazrī cites this and says the sūrah has been tried and tested successfully for this purpose. Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh Pānīpatī cites it in his Tafsīr Mazharī and says that his Shaykh, Mirzā Mazhar Jān-i-Jānān, instructed him to recite it at the time of fear and danger, saying its recitation has been tested and tried to avert all kinds of calamities and afflictions — and Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh says he has experienced it several times. This is transmitted as the experience of these scholars; it is reported here as they reported it.

## Living it

*The points below are reflections on the material above, not further reports from the tafsirs.*

**Notice the *Ilāf* in your own life.** The passage argues from the unremarkable — a trade route that worked, a road where no one troubled them. Allah drew the Quraysh's attention to something they lived with every year. The favours easiest to overlook are the ones we have had longest.

**Food and safety are the whole list.** By Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, ayah 4 comprehensively captures all that was needed for the Quraysh to live happily and peacefully in the world — something to eat, and nothing to fear. That reframes a great deal of what we call need.

**Let gratitude land on the Giver, not the gift.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 3 is that they should single Allah out for worship alone, with no idol, rival or statue beside Him. It is possible to revere a sacred place or a blessing and still not direct one's worship to the One behind it. Ayah 3 corrects the aim.

**Security is tied to obedience.** Ibn Kathir's principle is stated plainly: whoever accepts this command, Allah gives him safety in this life and the Hereafter; whoever disobeys, He removes both. The township of 16:112 had provision in abundance from every place — and tasted hunger and fear after turning ungrateful for it.

**Influence carries weight.** The narration that people follow Quraysh "in matters of good as well as in matters of evil" states the pattern in both directions. Whoever is looked to should weigh what he is teaching others to do.
